title: Housing by right on commercial land

definition.title: Housing by right on commercial land
definition.description: Apartment buildings (36+ homes per acre, at most one required parking space per home) allowed by right on land used for shops and offices. New construction, so counted in the Building Permits Survey measure.

source.citation: Texas SB 840, 89th Legislature (2025), enrolled text (Local Government Code chapter 218)

notes: Eligible land is read from parcel land use where a county has it (Pennsylvania: Philadelphia and Allegheny); elsewhere 'eligible land not measured'.
Cannot share a package with the TOD reforms: commercial land near stations is already TOD land.

parameters.label: Cap on apartments on commercial land, as a share of the county's baseline 5+ unit permits
parameters.rationale: The county's apartment market can rent only so many more homes in five years; the same kind of cap as the TOD reform.
parameters.revisit: Use Census SOMA absorption rates by metro.

parameters.label: Share of these commercial-land apartments the baseline would have permitted by rezoning or variance
parameters.rationale: Some commercial sites already get housing through rezoning, so the reform is credited only with the rest.
parameters.revisit: Count past rezonings of commercial parcels to residential in the parcel data.

parameters.label: Most parking spaces per home a town may require on commercial land

source.citation: Texas SB 840, 89th Legislature (2025), enrolled text, Local Government Code section 218.102(a)(2)(A): a municipality may not require "more than one parking space per dwelling unit"

parameters.rationale: The by-right rule caps required parking at one space per home (a cap, not a mandate).
parameters.revisit: Only if the modelled rule names another cap.

parameters.label: Share of apartments on commercial land that are new to the region
parameters.rationale: Some would have been built elsewhere in the region anyway; as the TOD net-new share.
parameters.revisit: Compare regional permit totals before and after a by-right commercial-land law.

parameters.label: Average land area of a commercial parcel
parameters.rationale: The parcel table counts parcels, not acres. Urban storefront lots are a tenth of an acre or less; strip centres and office parks are several acres. The range spans both.
parameters.revisit: Replace with measured parcel areas (OPA and Allegheny assessment lot sizes).

parameters.label: First-year share of full take-up (commercial land and conversions)
parameters.rationale: Projects already designed for commercial sites can file quickly; most start later.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on the permit ramp after a by-right commercial-land law.

parameters.label: Years until take-up on commercial land and conversions is full
parameters.rationale: Same form as the other reforms' ramps.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on the permit ramp after a by-right commercial-land law.

parameters.label: Share of commercial land that could take an apartment building within a few years
parameters.rationale: Underused parking lots, vacant stores and one-storey strip retail, not active or recently built buildings.
parameters.revisit: Measure from building age and improvement-to-land value ratios in parcel data.

parameters.label: Share of feasible commercial land redeveloped with apartments each year
parameters.rationale: Commercial sites change hands and are rebuilt more often than houses, but a by-right rule still takes years to reach builders; between the TOD (2%) and a fast-moving market.
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on permits after Texas SB 840 took effect (2025-09-01) once a year of data is published.

parameters.label: Price of an acre of commercial land, in median homes of the same tract
parameters.rationale: No commercial land prices are in the pack. A commercial acre is priced as a number of the tract's homes (a local price level from ACS home values), with an income-producing store or office at the high end and a vacant lot or parking lot at the low end.
parameters.revisit: Replace with assessed commercial land values per acre from parcel data.

parameters.label: Years after January 1, 2027 before commercial-land or conversion permits respond
parameters.rationale: Assumed in force on the first day of the window, like the benchmarks.
parameters.revisit: Set from a bill's effective date when one is modelled.

parameters.label: Homes per acre allowed by right on commercial land

source.citation: Texas SB 840, 89th Legislature (2025), enrolled text, Local Government Code section 218.102(a)(1): density no more restrictive than the greater of the highest residential density allowed or 36 units per acre; height the greater of the site's commercial height or 45 feet

parameters.rationale: The low end is Texas SB 840's floor of 36 homes per acre; a four-storey walk-up on a full commercial lot reaches 50-80.
parameters.revisit: Set from the density a modelled state bill names.

parameters.label: Development fees per unit, all major categories

source.citation: Housing Data and Technology Innovation Challenge, Participant Handbook, "Benchmark Policy Scenarios" and "The five scenarios"

parameters.rationale: The Handbook: "Teams should assume development fees total $50,000 per unit across all major fee categories."
parameters.revisit: Only if the Handbook changes.

parameters.label: Capitalisation rate used to value a finished mid-rise building
parameters.rationale: Larger, newer apartment buildings trade at somewhat lower cap rates than small ones.
parameters.revisit: Source from a published cap-rate survey for Pennsylvania metros.

parameters.label: Developer profit required on a mid-rise project, as a share of total cost
parameters.rationale: Developers and their investors typically need 10-20% on cost for larger projects.
parameters.revisit: Source from published feasibility studies.

parameters.label: Construction cost per square foot, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Wood or light-steel frame over a concrete podium costs more per square foot than small buildings; the range covers region and finish.
parameters.revisit: Look for a free public construction cost source.

parameters.label: Operating costs as a share of rent, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Vacancy, management, upkeep, insurance and property tax for a professionally run building.
parameters.revisit: Build from parts as for ADUs.

parameters.label: Soft costs as a share of construction, mid-rise apartment building
parameters.rationale: Design, permits, financing and other soft costs (other than the benchmark fee).
parameters.revisit: Source from published development pro formas.

parameters.label: Floor area per mid-rise apartment
parameters.rationale: New mid-rise apartments are mostly studios to two-bedrooms averaging about 850 sq ft.
parameters.revisit: Check against new multifamily construction characteristics (Census SOC).

parameters.label: Cost of one space in an above-ground parking structure

source.citation: UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies (February 2026), "No Such Thing as Free Parking", construction cost per space from 2025 Rider Levett Bucknall cost data for 17 U.S. cities, excluding land

parameters.rationale: Above-ground structures averaged about $52,000 per space across 17 cities, from $29,000 (Phoenix, Washington DC) to $99,000 (Portland), excluding land.
parameters.revisit: Check whether Philadelphia or Pittsburgh is among the 17 cities and use its value.

parameters.label: Cost of one surface parking space, land and construction

source.citation: Victoria Transport Policy Institute, Transportation Cost and Benefit Analysis II, chapter 5.4 "Parking Costs" (version of 3 October 2022), Table 5.4.4-1

parameters.rationale: The review's summary table puts surface parking land and construction at about $8,000 per space in 2022 dollars. Low covers cheap rural land; high covers urban land.
parameters.revisit: Update the price year to 2026 and check against a Pennsylvania cost estimate.

parameters.label: Parking spaces required per apartment under current rules
parameters.rationale: Common local minimums for apartments are one to two spaces per unit.
parameters.revisit: Replace with a sample of Pennsylvania zoning codes.

parameters.label: Premium over current value a mid-rise builder pays to assemble a site
parameters.rationale: Assembling several lots means paying holdouts above market; upzoning also raises asking prices (Chicago station-area land prices rose after upzoning).
parameters.revisit: Calibrate on station-area land sales after upzoning.

parameters.label: Construction cost per sq ft of the low-rise TOD prototype (variant)
parameters.rationale: A wood-frame walk-up has no elevator core, concrete podium or garage, so it costs less per square foot than the mid-rise (multifamily.hard_cost_per_sqft). Used only by the variant 'tod_lowrise'.
parameters.revisit: Price from published construction cost guides for garden and walk-up apartments.

parameters.label: Rent of a new mid-rise apartment as a multiple of the tract's two-bedroom median
parameters.rationale: New buildings with amenities near transit rent above the existing stock, most of which is decades old.
parameters.revisit: Compare new-lease asking rents with ACS medians near PA stations.

parameters.label: Two-bedroom rent as a multiple of median gross rent, where the two-bedroom median is blank
parameters.rationale: In Pennsylvania tracts the two-bedroom median is close to the all-units median gross rent.
parameters.revisit: Compute from ACS B25031 tracts that report both.
